title: The Church as field hospital
hook: Francis described the Church as a field hospital for the wounded
tomorrow: Doña Carmen wants to "put her house in order." what does that mean?

segments.voice: Last time, the scars the risen Jesus kept: healing takes time. Today, who does the healing, and where.

Not the hospital with a gift shop and a parking garage. A field hospital: a tent near the fighting, mud on the floor, the wounded carried in on stretchers. That's the picture Pope Francis reached for when he described what the Church should be. And Luke tells a story where a field hospital gets set up in the dirt. A man lies half dead on the road down to Jericho. A priest comes by, sees him, and crosses to the other side. A Levite does the same. Then a Samaritan, not the hero Jesus's listeners would expect, pulls up beside him.
screen: `A TENT NEAR THE FIGHTING.` → `HALF DEAD ON THE JERICHO ROAD.` → `THEN A SAMARITAN STOPS.`

segments.voice: What he does first is the whole point. He doesn't ask how the man got there, or whose side he's on, or what he did to deserve it. In the Douay-Rheims Bible, he "bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine." Then he lifts him onto his own animal, brings him to an inn, and pays for his care. Francis put it plainly in an interview: when someone is badly wounded, you don't ask about his cholesterol or his blood sugar. You heal the wounds first. Everything else can come after. Something worth repeating tonight: the parable isn't about priests being bad. It's about who stops, and Jesus gives the role to an outsider. A field hospital doesn't choose its patients. In a parish, it looks like a meal dropped off, a ride to a treatment, someone bringing communion to the homebound, a hall where a recovery group meets on folding chairs. Heal wounds first.
screen: `NO QUESTIONS FIRST.` · `OIL AND WINE ON THE WOUNDS.` · `NOT CHOLESTEROL: THE WOUND.` · `THE OUTSIDER STOPS.` · then, large: `HEAL WOUNDS FIRST.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who's hurting right now: someone sick, someone grieving, someone home alone. Send them a short message, or decide on one small thing you could bring them. Then let the sit hold them in mind, the way the Samaritan held the man steady on the road.
The Church as field hospital. Pope Francis's picture: a tent near the battle, treating wounds before asking questions.
screen: `THE CHURCH AS FIELD HOSPITAL — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: heal wounds first, the way the Samaritan did before asking a single question. Good night.

screen: `DAY 1716 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: DOÑA CARMEN WANTS TO "PUT HER HOUSE IN ORDER." WHAT DOES THAT MEAN?`

howItsDone: Catholic parishes carry out the field-hospital work through ministries to the sick and homebound, extraordinary ministers bringing communion, meal trains, Catholic Charities and hospital chaplains.

what a scholar hears: Francis's interview image of a field hospital after battle, read with Luke 10:30–35, where a Samaritan, an outsider to Jesus's listeners (John 4:9), binds the wounds.

Wait until you know the right words. Saying the wrong thing could make it worse.
Only if she asked for you. Field hospitals are for trained people, not friends.
chat.meaning: In Luke, the Samaritan treats the wound first, no speech. Francis's field hospital: go where someone's hurting and heal wounds first.

Samaritan.meaning: someone from Samaria, a people at odds with Jesus's Jewish listeners

Levite.meaning: a member of the tribe that served at the Temple

Jericho.meaning: a town down the road from Jerusalem

Pope Francis.meaning: the pope from Argentina who used the field-hospital picture

sources.quoted: bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine

sources.ref: Interview with Antonio Spadaro, 'A Big Heart Open to God' (the Church as a field hospital after battle)

notes: Luke 10:34 quoted from Douay-Rheims (Challoner); confirm exact wording.

Pope Francis's interview with Antonio Spadaro paraphrased (the Church as a field hospital after battle; you don't ask a seriously injured person about cholesterol and blood sugar; heal the wounds). The interview is under copyright, so no quotation marks. Confirm the paraphrase.

'Not the hero Jesus's listeners would expect' and the gloss 'a people at odds with Jesus's Jewish listeners' rest on John 4:9; the voice adds 'the parable isn't about priests being bad' to avoid making the priest and Levite a foil. Confirm a Jewish reader would find it fair.
